opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of my favorite connections, because it's one of those things that seems like a coincidence at first and then turns out to be pretty fundamental.

So if you start from a continuous-time state space model, you have a linear ODE, something like x'(t) = A x(t) + B u(t), and to actually run it on discrete data like a sequence of tokens, you have to discretize it with some step size, usually called delta. When you work through the standard discretization rules, say zero-order hold, in the simplest case of a scalar or diagonal system you get an update that looks like x_k = exp(delta A) x_{k-1} + (something proportional to delta) u_k. If you set A to be negative, say minus one, then exp(-delta) is a number between zero and one, and the input coefficient behaves roughly like one minus that. So you end up with x_k = (1 - g) x_{k-1} + g u_k, where g is a function of delta. That is exactly the form of a gated recurrence, a convex combination of the old state and the new input. It's essentially the gate in a GRU, or the forget and input gates in an LSTM.

The interpretation I find intuitive is that the step size controls how much attention you pay to the current input relative to the history. If delta is very large, you're taking a big step in time, the state basically resets, and you focus on the current input. If delta is very small, you're barely moving, so you mostly preserve the state and ignore the input. That's exactly what people have always said gates do: decide what to remember and what to forget.

What's nice is that this goes in both directions. On the RNN side, gating was mostly motivated heuristically, as a way to deal with vanishing gradients, and people found it empirically essential. The state space view gives a more principled explanation: gating is a discretization of an underlying continuous system, and the gate value is a learned, adaptive timescale. On the SSM side, the older models like S4 used a fixed delta that didn't depend on the input, so they were linear time-invariant. That made them efficient, since you could compute them as convolutions, but it limited what they could do, especially on tasks needing content-based reasoning, like selectively copying or ignoring certain tokens.

That was a big part of the motivation for Mamba and the selection mechanism. If the RNN people were right that gating is crucial, and gating is just discretization, then the natural move is to make delta, along with B and C, depend on the input. Then the model can decide token by token whether to absorb something into its state or let it pass. You lose the convolutional view, which is why we needed the hardware-aware parallel scan to keep it fast, but you gain the selectivity that gated RNNs had all along.

So I think of it as a kind of unification. Gating isn't just an engineering trick; it falls out naturally from viewing these models as discretized continuous-time systems, and that perspective tells you both why it works and how to generalize it.

r001.rationale: The response derives a gated recurrent update from discretizing a continuous-time state space model and says gating is a discretization of that system.

r002.rationale: It says a large time step makes the state nearly reset and shifts focus to the current input, meaning more forgetting of the previous state.

r003.rationale: It says a very small time step mostly preserves the state and causes the model to largely ignore the new input.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of my favorite things that came out of the Mamba work, because it was a connection that I think a lot of people had intuitions about but hadn't really been made precise.

So let me set it up. On the state space side, you start with a continuous-time system. You have a hidden state h of t, and its dynamics are governed by a differential equation: dh/dt equals A h plus B x. To actually run this on a computer, on discrete sequences, you have to discretize it. You pick a step size, delta, and you apply some discretization rule, zero-order hold, bilinear, whatever. And what falls out is a discrete recurrence, h_t equals A-bar h_{t-1} plus B-bar x_t, where A-bar is some function of delta and A. For zero-order hold it's literally exp of delta times A.

Now the key move in Mamba, the selectivity idea, is that we let delta depend on the input. So delta is no longer a fixed parameter, it's a function of x_t. And once you do that, something interesting happens. Take the simplest possible case: scalar A, say A equals negative one, and look at what A-bar becomes. It's exp of negative delta. If you parameterize delta the way we do, as a softplus of some linear projection of the input, then exp of negative delta turns out to be exactly one minus sigmoid of that linear projection. So A-bar is one minus a gate, and if you work out B-bar under the same discretization, it's the gate itself. So the recurrence becomes h_t equals one minus g_t times h_{t-1} plus g_t times x_t.

And that's just a gated RNN. That's essentially the update in a GRU, or the forget-gate-input-gate coupling you get in a simplified LSTM. The gate g_t is a sigmoid of a linear function of the input, which is literally how gates in RNNs have always been defined. So the thing that the RNN community arrived at heuristically, "let's have a sigmoid that controls how much to forget versus how much to write in," falls out of the state space view as a consequence of discretizing with an input-dependent step size.

The way I like to think about it conceptually is that delta is a notion of time, or really of resolution. A large delta means you're taking a big step, so the system moves a lot and the previous state gets forgotten quickly. A small delta means you barely move, you're essentially holding onto the previous state and ignoring the current input. And that is exactly what a gate is doing. A gate near one says "this input matters, overwrite," and a gate near zero says "skip this, preserve what I have." So forgetting and step size are the same mechanism viewed from two different directions. The RNN people called it gating, the control theory people called it discretization, and they are the same equation.

What I find nice about this is that it's not just a cute equivalence, it actually buys you something in both directions. From the SSM side, it gives you a principled reason why gating works: you're adaptively choosing how much of the continuous trajectory to traverse per token, which is a very natural thing to want for data like language where tokens are not uniformly informative. And from the RNN side, it tells you how to generalize gating to richer state structures. Once you see the gate as exp of negative delta times A, you can ask, well, what if A isn't a scalar? What if it's diagonal with many channels, or structured in some other way? Then you get a whole family of recurrences that are still fundamentally gated, but with much more expressive memory dynamics than a classical GRU would give you. And that's basically the design space that the selective state space models live in.

So the one-sentence version is: gating is what discretization looks like when you let the step size be data-dependent.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says gating is what discretization looks like with a data-dependent step size and derives the gated recurrence from an input-dependent discretization.

r002.rationale: It explains that a large step size means the previous state is forgotten quickly.

r003.rationale: It explains that a small step size means holding onto the previous state and ignoring the current input, so the new input has less influence.

astra-6.text:
One way to see the connection is to start with a continuous-time system. You have a state that evolves over time, and then you discretize that system to get a recurrence you can actually compute. The step size in that discretization controls how much the state changes at each update.

For a simple example, suppose the continuous-time dynamics move the state toward an input. When you discretize, you get an update that looks like a weighted combination of the old state and the new input. That’s also what a gate does in a recurrent neural network: it controls how much information you retain and how much new information you write.

So you can interpret certain gates as learning a discretization step size. A small step means the state barely changes—you preserve the memory. A large step means you move more quickly toward the new input. If that step size depends on the input, the model can decide how quickly to update based on what it’s seeing.

The precise correspondence depends on the dynamics and the discretization rule, so I wouldn’t say every gated RNN is exactly the same as a particular state space model. But mathematically, that’s a useful connection: gating gives you an adaptive timescale for the state.

r001.rationale: It describes a useful connection between gates and learned discretization step sizes, but does not state that gating and state-space discretization are mathematically equivalent; it explicitly qualifies that not every gated RNN matches a particular state-space model.

r002.rationale: It says a larger step moves the state more quickly toward the input, but does not connect longer elapsed time between inputs to greater forgetting of the previous state.

r003.rationale: It says a smaller step preserves memory and gives the new input less influence, but does not connect shorter elapsed time between inputs to that smaller influence.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to understand it is that a gate in an RNN is closely related to the step size you use to discretize a continuous-time system. Suppose you have a very simple state space model, where the hidden state satisfies dh/dt = −h + u. If you discretize that with a step size Δ, treating the input as constant over that interval, you get h_next = exp(−Δ) h + (1 − exp(−Δ)) u.

That looks exactly like a gated update: retain some fraction of the old state and mix in some fraction of the new input. The gate is controlling how much time effectively passes. A small step size means you mostly preserve your memory; a large step size means you move toward the new input.

So if you make that step size depend on the input, you get an input-dependent gate. That’s a useful connection because gating can look like an architectural trick, but from the continuous-time perspective, it has a very natural interpretation as an adaptive discretization. More general state space models have richer dynamics, so the correspondence isn’t always just a single scalar gate, but that basic intuition carries over.

r001.rationale: It derives the discretized state update and says it matches a gated update, presenting gating as adaptive discretization.

r002.rationale: It explains that a larger step size retains less of the old state and moves the state more toward the new input.

r003.rationale: It says a small step size mostly preserves memory, meaning each new input has less influence.
